slides.title: What is Abstraction?
slides.content: Abstraction hides implementation details and exposes only essential features. In C#, it is achieved using abstract classes and interfaces.

exercise.prompt: What is the main purpose of abstraction?
options: To hide complex implementation and expose essentials
exercise.answer: To hide complex implementation and expose essentials

slides.title: Abstract Classes
slides.content: An abstract class cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods (no body) and concrete methods (with body). Use the 'abstract' keyword.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition with a method that writes to the console; produces no output unless the method is invoked.

slides.title: Abstract Methods
slides.content: Abstract methods have no implementation. They must be overridden in a non-abstract derived class using the 'override' keyword.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

slides.title: Concrete vs Abstract Members
slides.content: Abstract classes can mix abstract members (must be overridden) with concrete members (inherited as-is). This promotes code reuse.

slides.title: Sealed Override
slides.content: A derived class can prevent further overriding of an abstract method by using 'sealed override'.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition with a method that writes to the console; produces no output unless the method is invoked.

slides.title: When to Use Abstraction
slides.content: Use abstraction when multiple classes share a common base but require different implementations of specific operations.

slides.title: Abstract Properties
slides.content: Abstract classes can also declare abstract properties. The derived class must implement the getter and/or setter.

slides.title: Abstraction Best Practices
slides.content: Name abstract classes with clear intent, keep them focused, and use them to define contracts for families of related types.
